questions.stem: Which Terraform address refers to the first counted Windows VM in CLZ-240?

options.A: azurerm_windows_virtual_machine.web[0]
options.B: azurerm_windows_virtual_machine.web[1]
options.C: azurerm_windows_virtual_machine.web["first"]
options.D: azurerm_windows_virtual_machine.web[*].first

optionExplanations.A: Counted resource indexes start at zero.
optionExplanations.B: Index 1 identifies the second instance.
optionExplanations.C: String keys belong to for_each, not this count pattern.
optionExplanations.D: A wildcard collection expression is not an individual resource address.

questions.stem: Why does the counted VM use azurerm_network_interface.web[count.index].id?

options.A: To assign every VM the first NIC simultaneously
options.B: To make the NIC's public IP become the VM password
options.C: To sort VMs according to current CPU usage
options.D: To pair each VM with the NIC at the same positional index

optionExplanations.A: The expression selects each current index rather than always zero.
optionExplanations.B: Networking identities are unrelated to passwords.
optionExplanations.C: Count indexes are configuration identities, not runtime metrics.
optionExplanations.D: The indexed reference aligns corresponding resource instances.

questions.stem: instance_count increases from two to three with existing values otherwise unchanged. What should the plan normally show for the indexed compute pattern?

options.A: Replacement of every existing VM merely because the count changes
options.B: Only an additional Role tag on the resource group
options.C: New third VM, NIC, public IP, and related association at index 2
options.D: An Azure Monitor autoscale rule without new VMs

optionExplanations.A: Unchanged earlier indexes need not be replaced.
optionExplanations.B: The variable controls counted resource instances.
optionExplanations.C: Increasing cardinality adds the new highest index and its dependencies.
optionExplanations.D: This lesson uses count and does not declare autoscaling.

questions.stem: Three counted VMs exist and instance_count becomes two. Which indexed VM is no longer described by configuration?

options.A: web[2]
options.B: web[0]
options.C: Whichever VM has the oldest Windows login
options.D: Whichever VM has the least CPU usage

optionExplanations.A: The remaining indexes are 0 and 1; the highest index falls outside the new count.
optionExplanations.B: The first index remains part of a count of two.
optionExplanations.C: Terraform uses addresses, not guest login history.
optionExplanations.D: Runtime CPU does not determine count identity.

questions.stem: A learner supplies instance_count = 2.5. Why is this not a valid instance count?

options.A: Terraform silently rounds every count up to three
options.B: Resource cardinality must be a whole number and the lesson validates it
options.C: Windows VMs always require an even count
options.D: The decimal automatically selects a VM size

optionExplanations.A: The lesson rejects fractions rather than rounding them.
optionExplanations.B: Fractional resource instances cannot be created.
optionExplanations.C: Odd whole-number counts are valid within the lesson bounds.
optionExplanations.D: Cardinality and size are separate inputs.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish lesson bounds from Terraform capability
questions.stem: Terraform count can be zero in some configurations. Why does instance_count = 0 fail in CLZ-240?

options.A: Terraform never supports zero instances
options.B: Azure requires exactly two VMs in every resource group
options.C: The lesson validates instance_count from one through five
options.D: A /32 NSG source requires at least one VM

optionExplanations.A: Count can conditionally omit resources with zero.
optionExplanations.B: That is not an Azure resource-group requirement.
optionExplanations.C: The lesson's educational and cost limits are narrower than generic count syntax.
optionExplanations.D: The prefix length does not define instance cardinality.

questions.stem: Can count depend on a new resource attribute that will be unknown until apply?

options.A: Yes; it can create an arbitrary number and sort them later
options.B: No; Terraform needs the count before remote resource creation
options.C: Yes; only the output list must be known in advance
options.D: No; because count can contain only literal numbers

optionExplanations.A: Terraform cannot plan an unknown cardinality that way.
optionExplanations.B: The graph requires a known number of instances during planning.
optionExplanations.C: Resource cardinality itself must be known.
optionExplanations.D: Known numeric expressions are also supported.

questions.stem: Which CLZ-240 expression makes all counted Windows VMs use the same selected size?

options.A: size = each.value.vm_size
options.B: size = count.index
options.C: size = azurerm_public_ip.web[count.index].ip_address
options.D: size = var.vm_size

optionExplanations.A: This lesson uses count, not a per-key object value.
optionExplanations.B: A numeric identity is not a valid VM SKU.
optionExplanations.C: An IP address is not a VM size.
optionExplanations.D: The resource repeats a single shared size input for every index.

questions.stem: Does count on the Windows VM block automatically duplicate the VNet and resource group?

options.A: No; only resource blocks with count are multiplied
options.B: Yes; every referenced resource inherits the same count
options.C: Yes; each disk requires an independent subscription
options.D: No; because counted VMs cannot use a VNet

optionExplanations.A: The VNet and resource group are separately declared shared resources.
optionExplanations.B: Meta-arguments do not propagate to other blocks.
optionExplanations.C: A disk does not require its own subscription.
optionExplanations.D: They use the shared subnet through their NICs.

questions.stem: The first counted VM name contains a suffix 1 while its state address ends [0]. Why is this consistent?

options.A: The name uses count.index + 1 while the Terraform index remains zero-based
options.B: Terraform changed the VM index after deployment
options.C: Azure always adds one to every Terraform resource address
options.D: The state is corrupt because names and indexes must match exactly

optionExplanations.A: Display naming can add one without changing the resource's state address.
optionExplanations.B: The naming expression does not renumber state.
optionExplanations.C: Azure names and Terraform addresses are different identifiers.
optionExplanations.D: There is no requirement for identical suffix and index.

questions.stem: Which lesson command directly lists Terraform's tracked indexed resource addresses?

options.A: az account show
options.B: Test-NetConnection
options.C: terraform fmt
options.D: terraform state list

optionExplanations.A: That reports account context rather than Terraform resource addresses.
optionExplanations.B: That tests network reachability.
optionExplanations.C: That formats configuration and does not list tracked objects.
optionExplanations.D: It displays addresses such as the VM, NIC, and public IP indexes.

questions.stem: CLZ-240 reports windows_vm_public_ips as one address per counted instance. What verification aligns with the goal?

options.A: Require all addresses to be identical
options.B: Confirm the output's cardinality matches instance_count and Azure's actual VM count
options.C: Require keys named web and ops
options.D: Treat the length of the resource-group name as the VM count

optionExplanations.A: Each counted public IP is a separate resource.
optionExplanations.B: The output and deployed inventory should agree.
optionExplanations.C: Those are named-map identities from the next lesson.
optionExplanations.D: A name's character length is unrelated to deployed instances.

questions.stem: A future count-based pattern gets VM names from a list. Removing the first list item shifts later items. Why can this be risky?

options.A: Terraform automatically recognizes names as immutable map keys
options.B: All count resources automatically become VMSS instances
options.C: Values can move to different numeric identities and cause unintended changes
options.D: Azure denies every changed list permanently

optionExplanations.A: Count uses indexes rather than names as keys.
optionExplanations.B: Count does not convert standalone VMs into a scale set.
optionExplanations.C: Positions remain the identities even when the associated list values shift.
optionExplanations.D: The risk is unintended changes, not a universal Azure prohibition.

questions.stem: The VM set evolves into distinct web, batch, and operations servers with different sizes. Which pattern is preferable?

options.A: count over a frequently reordered name list
options.B: for_each over a stable named map
options.C: One public IP resource with no VM definitions
options.D: Changing the global username after every insertion

optionExplanations.A: Reordering can change the values associated with indexes.
optionExplanations.B: Named identities suit distinct per-instance attributes and reduce positional churn.
optionExplanations.C: An IP resource cannot describe named server configurations.
optionExplanations.D: Usernames do not provide stable Terraform identity.

questions.stem: Why does CLZ-240 intentionally assign a Standard public IP to each counted NIC?

options.A: To keep independently reachable instances and explicit teaching egress while focusing on count
options.B: Because Terraform count cannot work with private NICs
options.C: Because every Windows VM must have an Internet-facing IP
options.D: Because public IPs eliminate the need for NSG rules

optionExplanations.A: The README labels this a teaching exception rather than the production management design.
optionExplanations.B: Count can repeat resources with private networking.
optionExplanations.C: Windows guests can operate with private NICs.
optionExplanations.D: Network policy remains necessary.

questions.stem: Which admin_cidr value fits the lesson's intended RDP access policy?

options.A: 0.0.0.0/0 to avoid updating an IP
options.B: One VM's private subnet /24 for Internet administration
options.C: The learner's current real public IPv4 /32
options.D: The Windows administrator username

optionExplanations.A: The universal source is intentionally rejected.
optionExplanations.B: That neither represents the real external administrator nor follows /32 scoping.
optionExplanations.C: The rule permits a single administrator source.
optionExplanations.D: A guest username is not a CIDR.

questions.stem: Why is the NIC-to-NSG association also counted with instance_count?

options.A: The NSG itself must have a different public IP for every rule
options.B: Windows disks require NSGs on their storage accounts
options.C: Counted VMs ignore subnet and NIC security policies
options.D: Every counted NIC needs the shared policy attached to its corresponding instance

optionExplanations.A: An NSG is not a public endpoint.
optionExplanations.B: This resource associates network interfaces, not disks.
optionExplanations.C: Count is a Terraform repetition mechanism and does not bypass Azure policy.
optionExplanations.D: The repeated association applies the common NSG consistently.

questions.stem: Why does adding another CLZ-240 instance increase more than just VM compute cost?

options.A: The pattern also adds a managed disk and a Standard public IP
options.B: Terraform charges a subscription fee per index
options.C: Every new instance duplicates the entire repository in Azure
options.D: The resource-group tag incurs an hourly charge

optionExplanations.A: Each counted set includes multiple billable Azure components.
optionExplanations.B: Terraform indexes are not billable Azure components.
optionExplanations.C: Repository files are not deployed as resource copies.
optionExplanations.D: Tags do not have their own hourly charge.

questions.stem: A vm_size string passes the lesson's regular expression. What still needs verification?

options.A: Only that the README contains the same text
options.B: Regional availability, subscription quota, and budget for the full count
options.C: That the chosen size appears in the public IP address
options.D: Nothing; a regular expression reserves Azure capacity

optionExplanations.A: Documentation text does not establish capacity.
optionExplanations.B: A valid-looking SKU string does not guarantee deployability.
optionExplanations.C: Public IPs do not encode VM size.
optionExplanations.D: Input syntax validation does not reserve resources.

questions.stem: Apply fails after creating part of the counted set because of quota. What should the learner do?

options.A: Delete the state immediately so Terraform forgets the failure
options.B: Assume failed apply rolled back every Azure object
options.C: Inspect state and the failure, then use the documented cleanup or a reviewed corrective plan
options.D: Increase count without checking quota

optionExplanations.A: That can orphan already created resources.
optionExplanations.B: Terraform does not guarantee automatic rollback of earlier creations.
optionExplanations.C: Partial creation must remain tracked and be handled deliberately.
optionExplanations.D: That worsens the capacity problem.

questions.stem: Traffic rises after CLZ-240 is deployed. Does count automatically add VMs?

options.A: No; its configured value changes only through Terraform configuration and apply
options.B: Yes; count reads CPU metrics by default
options.C: Yes; each public IP triggers one new server per request
options.D: No; Azure forbids scaling Windows VMs

optionExplanations.A: No demand-driven autoscale setting is declared here.
optionExplanations.B: Count has no default CPU policy.
optionExplanations.C: Public IPs do not manage compute scaling.
optionExplanations.D: Azure supports scaling; this specific pattern is manual.

questions.stem: When the count is increased, what should the saved plan be reviewed for besides new VM entries?

options.A: Only the number of blank lines in the configuration
options.B: Only whether the browser theme remains dark
options.C: Only whether the administrator username is hidden in the lesson title
options.D: Matching NICs, public IPs, associations, costs, and unexpected replacements

optionExplanations.A: Formatting is not the proposed Azure footprint.
optionExplanations.B: Theme state is unrelated to deployment.
optionExplanations.C: The title does not describe the full resource graph.
optionExplanations.D: The repeated resource graph should change coherently.

questions.learningObjective: Choose repetition within one resource block
questions.stem: Can a Windows VM resource declare both count and for_each to get numeric and named identities simultaneously?

options.A: Yes; Terraform multiplies the two values automatically
options.B: No; the two repetition meta-arguments are mutually exclusive on one block
options.C: Yes; but only for Windows Server 2022
options.D: No; because neither meta-argument can apply to Azure resources

optionExplanations.A: Terraform rejects the combination rather than multiplying it.
optionExplanations.B: Choose one instance identity model for that resource.
optionExplanations.C: The rule is Terraform syntax, not an operating-system feature.
optionExplanations.D: Both can apply individually to Azure resource blocks.

questions.learningObjective: Do not confuse OS provisioning with IIS configuration
questions.stem: CLZ-240's compute-count.tf creates Windows VMs without an IIS extension resource. What should a learner conclude?

options.A: Windows VM creation alone does not prove the IIS lesson page is installed
options.B: The Windows Server image guarantees the CLZ-200 page exists
options.C: The Standard public IP automatically installs IIS
options.D: The count index is an IIS site binding

optionExplanations.A: Guest web configuration requires an additional mechanism.
optionExplanations.B: The prior lesson's bootstrap is not inherited across separate configurations.
optionExplanations.C: Network addressing does not install guest roles.
optionExplanations.D: An index identifies a Terraform instance.

questions.stem: The counted set shares a generated administrator password. What remains essential?

options.A: Commit the password because there is more than one VM
options.B: Write the password into the public-IP output list
options.C: Protect state and explicit secret exports even when output is marked sensitive
options.D: Treat count.index as a substitute password

optionExplanations.A: Repetition does not reduce credential sensitivity.
optionExplanations.B: Output lists should not publish credentials.
optionExplanations.C: Terraform state can retain credentials for the entire set.
optionExplanations.D: An index is not an authentication credential.

questions.stem: What is the difference between web and web[1] for a counted Terraform resource?

options.A: They always refer to the same first instance
options.B: The first refers to the repeated resource collection; the second selects one instance
options.C: web[1] is the second Azure subscription
options.D: web is a private DNS zone while web[1] is a public record

optionExplanations.A: The index selects a distinct instance.
optionExplanations.B: Individual counted instances have numeric addresses.
optionExplanations.C: The index identifies a resource instance, not a subscription.
optionExplanations.D: These are resource references in the count lesson.

questions.stem: After terraform destroy, state is empty. Why also run az group exists for the captured group name?

options.A: To recreate the VMs if the group is missing
options.B: To automatically restore the last public IPs
options.C: To prove the VM size was available before apply
options.D: To verify the managed Azure resource group is gone, not only that local tracking is empty

optionExplanations.A: The command only reports existence.
optionExplanations.B: An existence query allocates nothing.
optionExplanations.C: The query is a cleanup check, not quota evidence.
optionExplanations.D: Cloud absence is separate evidence from local state contents.

questions.learningObjective: Choose the right scalable workload abstraction
questions.stem: The counted servers are interchangeable members serving one application. Which later pattern can better manage one scalable fleet?

options.A: One new subscription per count index
options.B: A Virtual Machine Scale Set
options.C: A Private DNS A record without compute
options.D: Renaming NICs after every web request

optionExplanations.A: Splitting subscriptions is not the fleet abstraction.
optionExplanations.B: VMSS is designed around a common instance model and scalable capacity.
optionExplanations.C: DNS can name endpoints but cannot manage a compute fleet.
optionExplanations.D: Dynamic naming does not provide fleet management.

questions.stem: A learner wants to remove the highest-index VM by deleting terraform.tfstate rather than changing count. Why is that unsafe?

options.A: The state file is the Azure VM's operating-system disk
options.B: Deleting state is identical to terraform destroy
options.C: Deleting state can only affect CSS preferences
options.D: It loses resource tracking without necessarily deleting the Azure objects

optionExplanations.A: State is metadata and values, not the guest OS disk.
optionExplanations.B: Destroy calls provider deletion operations; deleting a file does not.
optionExplanations.C: Terraform state is unrelated to the site's theme.
optionExplanations.D: Use a reviewed configuration change or destroy to manage infrastructure removal.

questions.stem: A learner runs the count-reduction exercise using terraform plan only. What happens to the existing Azure VMs?

options.A: The highest-index VM is immediately deleted by the plan
options.B: Every VM automatically restarts to read the plan
options.C: They remain unchanged until the reviewed plan is applied
options.D: The NSG temporarily opens all ports during planning

optionExplanations.A: Deletion requires an apply or destroy operation.
optionExplanations.B: The local planning command does not restart guests.
optionExplanations.C: Planning proposes deletions but does not execute them.
optionExplanations.D: Planning does not modify network rules.
